newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: New economic dynamism passes hard-hit Kazakhs by.
newsitem.headline: New economic dynamism passes hard-hit Kazakhs by.

text.p: A senior Kazakh minister has said she aimed to fight corruption, create a more transparent market and accelerate privatisation.
"Privatisation must take place quickly," Zhannat Yertlesova, the oil-rich republic's deputy finance minister and head of a powerful government think-tank, told Reuters on Wednesday.
"But there has to be effective control over contracts to make sure both sides fulfil their obligations."
Facing big problems over mounting debts to employees and pensioners, the Kazakh government is rolling forward a fire-sale of choice oil and gas enterprises to try and fill empty state coffers.
A United Nations survey published last month said foreign direct investment in the republic totalled $3.24 billion in mid-1996, more than double the 1994 figure.
Yertlesova also dismissed widespread popular doubts over the sell-off, which -- rare for a former Soviet republic -- is mainly to foreign companies.
"I have no problem with foreign ownership," said Yertlesova. "The main thing is that there is an owner."

But foreign investors have eyed the resource-rich republic, the size of western Europe, with caution, complaining of a lack of transparency in the privatisation process and alleging widespread corruption.
Last week, a U.S.-funded opinion poll showed 91 percent of the 16.9 million population considered official corruption a "serious problem".
"I think corruption is a big problem and there are shortcomings," Yertlesova said. "But we're now starting on revolutionary structural reform to place tougher controls on officials."
Yertlesova said the government aimed to beat its own annual inflation target this year, hoping to clock in annual price rises at 15 percent rather than the targeted 17 percent.
Western analysts said the target was achievable but they worried over rumours the government might pay off over 30 billion tenge ($400 million) in pension arrears in one go.
One Western analyst warned: "If the government decides to pay off pension arrears, then no inflation target is achievable."
Following a succesful $200 million Eurobond debut in December, Yertlesova said Kazakhstan planned to tap international markets again this year for funds to form the basis of new pension funds.
Western sources say the republic could go to the market as early as June, but warn any debt issue linked so directly to pension or wage arrears could put off foreign investors.
A new dynamism has gripped the Kazakh economy in recent months, but people often have to wait months for meagre salaries or pensions and many believe reforms have passed them by.

Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev, worried by sinking popularity over the government's payments crisis, earlier this month threatened to sack his reformist prime minister if he failed to redress the wage and pension backlog by April 10.
Nazarbayev appeared to withdraw the threat but popular discontent continues to overshadow the reform process. Trade Unions plan a nation-wide protest on March 30.
"The state's debt to workers is a big sum, around 60 billion tenge ($800 million)," said Leonid Solomin, a well-known trade union leader. "There is a serious risk of a social explosion," he said.
